newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales to keep up pressure for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales to keep up pressure for rate rise.

text.p: Another robust set of British retail sales data suggest consumers are growing less resistant to price rises and will keep up pressure on the authorities to raise interest rates swiftly after the May 1 election.
Retail sales grew 0.3 percent in March, although revisions to back months allowed the year-on-year growth rate to drop to 4.0 percent versus 4.3 percent in February.

"With signs consumers are growing less price sensitive and our expectation that retail sales growth will pick up to around 5.0 percent this year, this is not good news for inflation," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.

Retail sales figures showed a massive jump in spending on clothing and footwear in March -- up 1.6 percent on the month -- while the retail prices report last week showed prices in that sector jumped 2.0 percent in the period.

"The RPI report showed that shops are not passing on falling cost pressures and collapsing producer prices to customers, and it is disappointing that retailers have succeeded in getting the price increases to stick," said Cole.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has justified his decision not to raise interest rates from 6.0 percent by citing the fact that falling producer prices have yet to feed through to the high street.
But other economists said while some higher pricing has stuck, it is within an overall picture of very subdued inflation.
"To a certain extent the strength of demand is allowing shops to push up prices, but this is taking place within a very competitive pricing regime," said Alex Garrard, economist at UBS.
"So while prices are creeping up, the key ones like clothing and footwear and household goods are comfortably below the overall rate of inflation."
Minutes of the March 5 monetary meeting between Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George, also released on Wednesday, show Clarke citing price competition as keeping a lid on prices.

"Consumers were still cautious and competition among retailers remained strong, especially among supermarkets," the minutes reported. George advised him to raise rates by a quarter point at the meeting, but Clarke declined saying the upside risk of unsustainably strong consumer demand had eased somewhat since the last meeting.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, said rates need to go up immediately after the election if the government has any change of meeting its 2.5 percent inflation target.

"Four percent year-on-year growth in retail sales is in itself inconsistent with the inflation target. Added to that is the fact that in April consumers will be that much richer," he said, referring to the income tax cut announced in November and implimented in April, and the first building society windfall payment sent out to customers this week.
